items.title: F-35C completes first launch and recovery trials on a Ford-class carrier
items.summary:
Two Navy F-35C Lightning II fighters have completed the jet’s first round of launch and recovery testing aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy, the Navy’s second Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, Lockheed Martin said Thursday .

Over 11 days of testing that began Oct. 13, the Navy’s 251st birthday , the two jets made 34 flights and logged 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings, the company said. The aircraft belong to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23, or VX-23, known as the “Salty Dogs,” at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland.

The flights were part of Kennedy’s Aircraft Compatibility Testing, which assesses how the ship’s launch and recovery equipment works with Navy aircraft, according to the Navy. The first arrested landing came on Oct. 13 , and the first catapult launch on Oct. 14 , Navy photo captions show.

Unlike Nimitz-class carriers, which launch and recover aircraft with steam catapults and hydraulic arresting gear, Ford-class carriers use the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System , or EMALS, and the Advanced Arresting Gear , or AAG. Lockheed said EMALS allows smoother, more precisely controlled launches, while AAG can handle a broader range of recovery conditions.

The Ford class also has a smaller island, the tower that houses the bridge and flight control, set about 140 feet farther back than on Nimitz-class ships. Lockheed said the island and a redesigned flight deck change airflow, exhaust patterns and deck operations.

items.t: F-35C completes first launch and recovery trials on a Ford-class carrier

items.title: Hegseth, in Caracas, announces US-Venezuela military partnership agreement
items.summary:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new agreement on military cooperation with Venezuela on Wednesday as he made his first visit to the country since U.S. special forces deposed President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid in Caracas.

Hegseth announced the agreement alongside Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodriguez, who welcomed him to the presidential palace. He said it covered joint training, intelligence sharing and other aspects of U.S.-Venezuelan military cooperation. Rodriguez said the arrangement would help confront “common threats” and strengthen training for Venezuela’s armed forces. 

Hegseth said the partnership would herald a significant ramp-up in joint action against drug trafficking groups.

“To the narco terrorists who have used this as a safe haven, your time is up. We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you,” Hegseth said, speaking from the U.S. embassy.

Washington already holds growing influence in Venezuela, particularly in the oil sector. Since Maduro’s removal, U.S. officials have moved quickly to shape the country’s future, focusing on energy policy and investment. 

That role expanded sharply in August under a deal granting producer North American Blue Energy Partners, or NABEP, long-term access to 17 oilfields that contain about a fifth of the country’s oil reserves through a partnership with the U.S. government. The United States secured a 35% stake in NABEP’s parent, a guaranteed share of output and first refusal rights on the remainder.

items.title: Air Force relieves Eglin security forces squadron commander
items.summary:
The commander of a security forces unit located at a Florida Air Force base was relieved from his post this week due to a loss of confidence .

Lt. Col. Michael Bruton, commander of the 96th Security Forces Squadron, was removed from command earlier this week due to a “lack of confidence in his ability to lead,” an Eglin Air Force Base spokesperson told to Military Times. 

The spokesperson did not say what prompted the removal or caused the lack of confidence in Bruton’s leadership. 

The spokesperson declined to comment on who made the decision to relieve Bruton or whether anyone was placed as interim commander in the meantime.

The news of Bruton’s relief comes two months after the unit found a burnt vehicle with a deceased individual inside at the edge of the base while on a routine patrol. Although the car and individual, later identified as Senior Airman Tamera Moniq Bolden-Cleckley, 26, were not on the main base, the intersection is part of the Test and Training Range Complex, which is federal property of the Department of the Air Force.

The Air Force Office of Special Investigations and the Okaloosa County Sheriff’s Office are still investigating the incident.

The 96th Security Forces Squadron , based at Eglin in Florida , is tasked with securing and defending the base’s weapons systems, air base assets, personnel and resources.

items.t: Air Force relieves Eglin security forces squadron commander

items.title: New Army contract for bunkers in Middle East cites ‘extreme operational urgency’
items.summary:
The Army urgently needs to build concrete bunkers to replace shipping containers and T-walls that troops are using to shelter from drones across the Middle East, contract documents show.

The service needs contractors to build “fully operational indirect fire” bunkers in 45 days “due to extreme operational urgency,” according to a solicitation posted Nov. 13 to the federal government’s contracting database. 

“Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace non-standard personnel protection shelters,” Army officials wrote in contracting documents. “The objective is to safeguard U.S. and Coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in the [U.S. Central Command] Area of Responsibility.” 

The Army also asked contractors to demolish and dispose of “non-standard bunkers” (identified as “converted” shipping containers), T-walls, and “scrap obstacles” in order to make room for the new concrete structures. The concrete buildings will also have sandbag reinforcements — a modification that troops have made to shelters in recent years to mitigate blast overpressure waves . 

In all, contract documents indicate that the service needs five bunkers at two bases in Saudi Arabia, 47 at two sites in Lebanon and 10 at a site in Israel. Army Times’ Michael Peck was first to report on the contract posting.

items.t: New Army contract for bunkers in Middle East cites ‘extreme operational urgency’

items.title: VA raised Oracle’s contract cap to $27B. Auditors still can’t verify the cost of the rollout.
items.summary:
VA plans to double its electronic health record rollout in 2027 as federal auditors wait for the records to show the math behind its $56.5 billion estimate.

The Department of Veterans Affairs raised the ceiling on Oracle’s electronic health record contract by $17 billion in September and plans to install the system at more than twice as many medical centers next year. Federal auditors told senators at a Nov. 18 hearing that they still lack the records they need to judge what the program will cost in total, or whether the VA can finish the rollout by its scheduled date of 2031. 

The Government Accountability Office has waited more than a year for the analysis behind the VA’s $56.5 billion long-term estimate. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said committee staff learned about the contract increase through news reports before it appeared in their regular briefings or contract notifications. Dr. Neil Evans, who leads the VA’s electronic health record modernization office, said the omission was inadvertent.

When lawmakers asked GAO how much they believe the project will cost, they were not able to answer.

“I can’t say for sure how much higher because we haven’t seen the underlying documentation,” Carol Harris, GAO’s director of information technology and cybersecurity, told the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee. “But do I think the costs are going to go up? The answer is yes.”

items.title: Defense Business Brief: Vantor’s Raptor; Hadrian’s foundry, and more
items.summary:
Flying drones at lower altitudes can help them evade radar detection, but what happens if the GPS is jammed? How will the drone know where it is?

“The lower you go, the more important it is that you're looking out obliquely…you need to have a 3D reference in order to be able to compare to, to determine your position,” Paul Millhouse, Vantor’s senior director who leads the Raptor program, told Defense One. 

Drones typically use vision-based positioning informed by two-dimensional maps that display an area from an overhead perspective, Millhouse explained. But buildings can become more than just rooftops in a drone’s line of sight when flying low through a cityscape at lower altitudes. 

Using its three-dimensional satellite imagery, Vantor built its Raptor technology to be a GPS alternative so drones can navigate even if signals are jammed. The technology uses a video feed from the drone’s on-board camera and an initial estimate of that camera’s position and altitude, which is maintained by the drone’s navigation system.

The company first debuted the product last year and has been busy flight testing and integrating it in “live, real GPS-jammed environments,” including long-range operations…

Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara made the announcements Tuesday at a press conference after the 37th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group at NATO headquarters in Brussels.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to announce the offer Thursday in Berlin at a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” of Ukraine supporters, where U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steven Witkoff are expected to brief European leaders on peace negotiations.

Ukraine is forging ahead with its long-range strike campaign with support from European partners, despite Washington’s request to prioritize front-line defense and associated midrange strikes instead.

items.title: Japanese nuclear submarines are a bad idea for East China Sea security — for now
items.summary:
Japan faces a difficult security environment. Relations with the rising superpower next door, namely China , are extremely tense at present and for the last year. Japan must also contend with a hostile Russia and North Korea as well. All three of these countries possess nuclear weapons and are actively adding to those arsenals. If that wasn’t enough, the second Trump administration has been distracted by the Middle East and also demonstrated a relatively carefree approach to traditional U.S. allies.

No wonder that nuclear talk is now fashionable among defense analysts in Tokyo.

Indeed, Japan has good reasons to take its defense more seriously and has set about doing so. For decades, Tokyo restricted itself to spending about 1% of GDP on defense, but that self-imposed restriction fell away in recent years. Today, serious calculations are underway regarding whether or not Japan should follow other middle powers like Australia and South Korea by creating a nuclear submarine program. While the idea is not without merit, Japanese and American strategists need to consider the wider consequences before stepping out on this new initiative.

In early November, the Chinese newspaper Global Times published an editorial revealing that China’s rather predictable reaction to any Japanese plan to build a nuclear submarine force would be extremely harsh. The U.S. Air Force is stepping up its training on the country’s westernmost islands as it seeks to develop more places from which to project power and monitor adversaries across the Pacific and the Arctic.

Those efforts were visible in late October, when airmen deployed to Shemya Island in Alaska’s Aleutian Islands for a rare exercise, and when the Air Force released a proposal outlining its plans for operations on islands near Guam.

On Shemya, which is closer to Russia than to mainland Alaska , F-16s, tankers and cargo planes deployed to Eareckson Air Station from Oct. 18 to Oct. 26. While there, the jets “sat alert,” with crews in position and maintaining readiness to launch on short notice. 

“While it was commonplace for aircraft to sit alert in the 1980s, this deployment marks the first time in decades that aircraft have sat alert at Eareckson,” Capt. Kitsana Dounglomchan, Alaskan NORAD Region spokesperson, said in an email.

The Shemya deployment ended with long-range operations as part of a U.S.-Canada homeland-defense exercise. As F-16s launched from Eareckson to cover the southern portion of the Alaska theater of operations, F-35s and F-16s at Eielson Air Force Base 1,600 miles to the west took off to cover the northwest portion of the theater. Canadian CF-18s flew from their base at Cold Lake, 2,600 miles from Shemya, to cover the northern part.

items.title: The Coast Guard icebreaker nobody wanted just came back from a 133-day Arctic patrol
items.summary:
Second chances don’t come around too often, but they did for the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Storis, an icebreaker that started life as a failed towboat for offshore oil rigs but joined America’s maritime security service in 2024–despite one Coast Guard admiral saying at one point that the ship “may, at best, marginally meet our requirements.”

On Saturday, the ship returned to its temporary home port of Seattle after a 133-day, 17,000-nautical-mile deployment where Storis was the only U.S. surface ship in the High Arctic , the region’s northernmost section, according to a Coast Guard press release .

Along the way, the crew carried out the first law enforcement mission by an icebreaker in more than 20 years when they inspected fishing boats in the Bering Sea. They also practiced firing machine guns in extreme cold conditions; escorted a grounded fishing vessel to safety; tested out small drones in extreme cold and at high latitudes; and monitored Chinese-flagged research vessels, which experts say gather oceanographic information for China’s scientific, commercial and military fleets.

Europe is beginning to explore the possibility of delivering conventional military payloads from orbit , with the German arm of defense behemoth MBDA and space transportation company ATMOS Space Cargo teaming up to investigate a concept known as Precision Orbital Deep Strike (PODS). The proposal involves putting military payloads into space before sending them back through the atmosphere when commanded, potentially offering a radically different approach to long-range precision strike.

The concept is undoubtedly hugely ambitious. Getting a payload into orbit and returning it to Earth is a very different problem from developing a reliable weapon capable of striking a designated target with precision and at a predictable time. items.title: What AI’s rebrand to ‘super intelligence’ means for the Pentagon
items.summary:
The Defense Department renamed its office dedicated to advancing artificial intelligence across the military to reflect President Donald Trump’s rebranding of the technology. 

The Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office will now be called the Super Intelligence Office, or SIO, according to a recent announcement . 

In the statement, Cameron Stanley , the Pentagon’s senior official for applied AI critical technology, called the redesignation “a clear signal” of where his department is going. 

“We have moved beyond experimental prototypes,” he said. “As the Super Intelligence Office, our mission is to harness the full power of sovereign Super Intelligence to ensure decisive military superiority across every domain.” 

The term “sovereign,” as it applies to AI, refers to a model governed within a specific boundary set by a nation or organization. 

However, the name change appears to get ahead of the technology itself. Although super intelligence is a recognized concept in AI research, experts say it remains a theoretical possibility rather than an existing capability.

The switch to “super intelligence” 

In September, Trump signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace the term “artificial intelligence,” as defined by federal law, with “super intelligence.” 

“We’re going to be naming it SI, super intelligence. We don’t want to hear artificial because it’s not artificial. It’s very powerful. It’s brilliant,” Trump said just ahead of the signing.

items.t: What AI’s rebrand to ‘super intelligence’ means for the Pentagon

items.title: US Navy used expired munitions during Iran war, Cao says
items.summary:
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told lawmakers Tuesday that the U.S. Navy recoded and fired missiles he described as “expired” during the war with Iran. 

Cao made the disclosure during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on his nomination to become Navy secretary, saying some of the munitions used during Operation Epic Fury and the Iran war had been previously classified as unserviceable. 

“A lot of the munitions we used in Epic Fury, we were able to recode those,” Cao said. “They were code echo, code foxtrot, which means they’re expired. But, you know, I came from a poor family, right? Things like bread doesn’t [sic] expire. You just rub some water on it, microwave it for 15 seconds and it’s good to go.”

Code echo and foxtrot both refer to materiel that is classified as “unserviceable” but able to be fixed, according to the Defense Logistics Agency manual.

Echo specifically means materiel that requires limited effort to restore, while foxtrot means materiel that requires repair and overhaul.

The U.S. military has faced concerns over a potential munitions shortage after it launched a significant chunk of its Tomahawk long-range cruise missiles during the opening salvo of Operation Epic Fury and throughout the Iran war.

In March, the Washington Post reported that the U.S. military had burned through at least 850 Tomahawk missiles after the first month of Operation Epic Fury.

At the time, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated in a report that the U.S. still had 3,000 left.

items.title: Flying Stripped-Down F-15 “Silver Eagles” To Their Limits
items.summary:
Driving across the vast flightline at Robins Air Force Base in Georgia, a prominent hangar bears the title “Welcome to Eagle Country.” A row of nearby smaller ‘barn’ hangars each reveals the telltale silhouette of an F-15 inside it, which on closer inspection are a mixture of either immaculate gray-painted or stripped-down bare metal Strike Eagles . The howl of one of the F-15E’s jet-fuel starters is followed by the sound of its engines spooling up. In the front seat, a pilot from the lesser-known 339th Flight Test Squadron based here is taking one of the bare metal jets up for a test flight.

The Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex here has performed program depot maintenance, known as PDM, on F-15s since 1975 and this critical support of the U.S. Air Force’s Eagle fleet continues today. The C-5M Galaxy , C-17 Globemaster , and C-130 Hercules fleets also receive deep maintenance here.

Roughly every seven years an F-15 comes to Warner Robins for PDM in the large Air Logistics Complex hangars, where it gets stripped down to the bare bones. The airframe is thoroughly checked over, the latest upgrades are added, and the jet is repaired where necessary by the hardworking depot maintenance team.

With just two squadrons of F-15C/Ds remaining, that fleet has been managed to retain airframes that don’t require PDM. Therefore, the deep maintenance at Robins is now dedicated to F-15E Strike Eagles, with new F-15EXs set to start cycling through in the next few years.

items.t: Flying Stripped-Down F-15 “Silver Eagles” To Their Limits

CAMP also aligns with Air Force efforts to expand its organic ground-based air defenses , which it has historically relied on the Army to provide.

items.title: Major AI platforms generated viable plans for terrorist attacks, GAO finds

According to a Government Accountability Office report published Wednesday, investigators tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok in spring 2026. They found that all four platforms provided information that could help malicious actors plan and carry out attacks.

In each case, the investigators were able to circumvent the platforms’ safety guardrails by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques.

“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work. And I think that’s the story here,” Kevin Walsh, a director of IT and cybersecurity at GAO, said in a podcast interview published alongside the report.

items.title: Troops in unsafe barracks can get temporary housing on or off base, Pentagon says
items.summary:
Troops living in barracks with “emergency conditions” that pose health or safety risks can get temporary lodging on or off base, according to new rules set by the Pentagon. 

In a Nov. 10 memo, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth directed the services to follow barracks standards laid out in October by the Assistant Secretary of War for Energy, Installations, and Environment, Mark Dale . The new guidelines classify barracks maintenance work orders into three categories: emergency, urgent and routine. 

The memo did not provide specific examples of what scenarios would classify under the three categories. Barracks have become a highly scrutinized quality-of-life issue in recent years, with troops facing problems that range from mold and pest infestations impacting their health to serious safety concerns as well as more routine nuisances like broken air conditioners in hot climates and delayed maintenance on aging buildings .

The military services were told to inspect barracks by Monday and take actions to address “emergency conditions” within 24 hours, which includes providing troops with temporary quarters if their room isn’t “safe” enough to live in.

Rob Evans, founder of the barracks review app, Hots&Cots , and an advocate for junior enlisted housing, said the urgency behind these instructions is right, but “service members have been through this before.”

The new order, issued Nov. 5 and effective immediately, replaces an existing version issued August 2024 . It was signed by Lt. Gen. Thomas Feltey, who took over command of V Corps this fall.
